title: Free and discounted things to do in New Jersey after 60
dek: Park passes, half-price train rides, tuition-free college classes and free museums. Here is what New Jersey residents 60 and older can get for little or nothing, and how to claim it.
keyFacts: NJ residents 62+ can get a free State Park Senior Citizen Pass at any park office.
NJ Transit riders 62+ pay half the regular one-way fare with valid ID.
State law (N.J.S.A. 18A:62-3) lets public colleges waive tuition for residents 65+ when seats are open. Fees still apply.
The federal Senior Pass costs $80 for life or $20 a year, for ages 62+.
Princeton University Art Museum, the Zimmerli and the New Jersey State Museum charge no admission.
body:
Turning 60 in New Jersey does not come with a welcome basket. It does come with a long list of quiet perks. Most of them are never advertised. You have to know they exist and ask.

This guide collects the best free and discounted options we could verify, from state parks to college classrooms. Each section tells you who qualifies, what it costs and what to bring. Ages vary from program to program, so check the age on each one before you go.

Which park passes should I get first?

The New Jersey State Park Senior Citizen Pass

If you are a New Jersey resident aged 62 or older, you can get a free Senior Citizen Pass for free entrance to state parks. You pick it up at any state park office. Bring a driver's license or other ID that shows your age and New Jersey address. For questions, the State Park Service information line is 1-800-843-6420.

This pass pays off fast. Several of the most popular parks charge entrance fees in summer, including Island Beach State Park in Ocean County. Get the pass in the off season, when park offices are quiet, and keep it in the car.

The federal America the Beautiful Senior Pass

The National Park Service sells a Senior Pass to U.S. citizens and permanent residents aged 62 or older. A lifetime pass costs $80. An annual pass costs $20, and you can later upgrade it to the lifetime version in person. The pass covers entrance fees at national parks and other federal recreation sites that charge them.

New Jersey has several places where it helps. The Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge in Galloway charges $4 per car for its 8-mile Wildlife Drive and honors the interagency passes. Its visitor center, open Wednesday through Sunday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m., sells passes for cash or check only. Gateway National Recreation Area at Sandy Hook, Thomas Edison National Historical Park in West Orange and Morristown National Historical Park are all federal sites as well.

  1. Buy in person if you can. More than 1,000 federal sites sell the pass, and you walk out with it in hand.
  2. Or buy a digital pass. Recreation.gov sells a digital version you can save to your phone and use right away.
  3. Mail order is slowest. The USGS online store ships physical passes, which can take up to three weeks. A receipt does not work as a pass while you wait.

Fishing without a license

New Jersey residents aged 70 and older do not need a freshwater fishing license. Your driver's license or other proof of age serves as your license, and you still follow all the regular fishing rules. Residents 70 and older also do not need a trout stamp. If you are under 70, check current license types and prices with NJ Fish and Wildlife at 609-292-2965 before you buy. Saltwater fishing works differently. Anglers 16 and older register online with the state's Saltwater Recreational Registry instead of buying a license.

How do senior fares work on NJ Transit?

NJ Transit gives riders aged 62 and older a reduced fare of half the regular one-way fare. It works on trains, buses and light rail. One exception: for travel to or from Metro-North stations, the senior age is 65.

You do not need a special card. You do need a valid ID that shows your date of birth and was issued by a government, social service or transit agency. NJ Transit accepts a long list of IDs, including:

  • Your Medicare card
  • A driver's license or state non-driver ID
  • A passport
  • An NJ Transit Reduced Fare ID
  • A county or military ID

To buy, choose the "Senior/Passenger with Disability" ticket type on a ticket vending machine or in the NJ Transit mobile app. You can also show your ID at a ticket office or to the bus driver, light rail operator or train conductor. On private interstate buses that are not marked NJ Transit, you must also hand over a Reduced Fare Coupon on each ride.

A round trip to Manhattan at half fare is one of the best deals in the state. Keep your Medicare card handy.

If you no longer drive, ask about your county's senior transportation service too. Most counties run one for medical trips, shopping and senior centers. The statewide Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 can connect you to your county office on aging.

Can I really take college classes for free at 65?

Yes, with some fine print. A New Jersey law, N.J.S.A. 18A:62-3, allows the boards of public colleges and universities to waive tuition for residents aged 65 and older. Each school writes its own policy, so the details differ. Two real examples show how it works.

William Paterson University lets any New Jersey resident aged 65 or over enroll in regularly scheduled courses if classroom space permits. The course also needs enough tuition-paying students to run. You still pay application fees and mandatory and course-related fees, such as technology fees. You may register only on the first day of the semester, and you file a new application and waiver form, with a government ID, every semester.

Rowan College at Burlington County waives tuition for seniors aged 65 and older who live in Burlington County. Fees are not waived. Seniors register on a space-available basis on or after the first day of classes, and you must show proof of age and residency first. If you register early, you pay full tuition, and the waiver is not applied after the fact.

Common mistakes

Registering early by accident, which triggers full tuition. Assuming fees are covered. Forgetting that a popular class may be full by the first day. Call the registrar or bursar before the semester and ask, in plain words, "How does your senior tuition waiver work?"

Most seniors audit, which means you attend without grades or credit. Ask whether auditing changes the fees. For noncredit options built for older learners, see our guide to learning something new in New Jersey.

Which museums are free?

Some of the best art and history collections in the state cost nothing to enter.

  • Princeton University Art Museum, Princeton. Admission is free to all. It is open every day, with hours until 8 p.m. on Thursdays and Fridays. It closes on Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year's Day and the Fourth of July.
  • Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers, New Brunswick. Admission is free and general visits need no reservation. It sits at 71 Hamilton Street on the Rutgers campus. It is open Wednesday through Sunday, with Thursday hours until 8 p.m., and closed Mondays and Tuesdays.
  • New Jersey State Museum, Trenton. General admission is free. It is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., at 205 West State Street. Planetarium shows cost extra, $10 for adults, and seniors 65 and older get $1 off.

Other museums offer free days. WheatonArts in Millville, for example, takes part in Bank of America's Museums on Us program on the first full weekend of each month for that bank's cardholders. Many local libraries also lend free or discounted museum passes. Ask at the circulation desk.

What do libraries and county parks offer?

Your public library may be the best free resource in town. New Jersey libraries run book clubs, movie afternoons, lectures, craft groups, chair yoga and one-on-one tech help. In tax season, many host free AARP Foundation Tax-Aide preparation for older and low-to-moderate income filers. Ask for a printed events calendar, or sign up for the email list.

County park systems are the other hidden gem. They run guided nature walks, birding outings, garden talks and concerts, many of them free. A few standouts:

  • Cape May County Park and Zoo in Cape May Court House has free admission to the park and zoo, with about 550 animals.
  • Frelinghuysen Arboretum in Morris Township is open every day from 8 a.m. to sunset and has paved paths through its gardens.
  • Batsto Village in Wharton State Forest is free on most days. Weekends from Memorial Day to Labor Day carry a $5 fee for New Jersey residents.

For more ideas, see our list of 20 easy day trips in New Jersey.

How do I claim all of this in one afternoon?

Most of these perks take a single trip and the right ID. Here is a simple order of operations that works for most people over 62.

  1. Gather your ID. Put your driver's license or state ID and your Medicare card in one place. Between them they cover the park pass, NJ Transit and most museum or ticket desks.
  2. Stop at a state park office. Pick up the free Senior Citizen Pass. Call 1-800-843-6420 first if you are unsure which office is staffed.
  3. Decide on the federal pass. If you will visit Forsythe, Sandy Hook or a national park out of state more than a few times, the $80 lifetime pass usually pays for itself.
  4. Call your library. Ask about museum passes, the events calendar and free tax help in the spring.
  5. Call your county office on aging. Ask about senior transportation, senior center programs and any county park discounts.
  6. Check the money programs. If your income is modest, look at PAAD, Lifeline and the PAS-1 property tax relief form before anything else.

Which discounts should I ask about?

The largest savings for many older New Jerseyans are not on fun at all. They are on bills. Before you chase a 10 percent coffee discount, make sure you are not missing these:

ProgramWho it helpsKey figure
PAADPrescription costs$5 generic / $7 brand copay for income under $54,943 single, $62,390 married
LifelineUtility bills$225 a year, same income rules as PAAD
PAS-1 property tax reliefANCHOR, Senior Freeze, Stay NJApply by November 2, 2026
NJ Transit senior fareRiders 62+Half the regular one-way fare

For the details, read our guides to prescription and bill help and property tax relief. The PAAD hotline is 1-800-792-9745.

After that, make asking a habit. Movie theaters, restaurants, hardware stores, pharmacies and hotels often have senior rates that are not posted. The age can be 55, 60, 62 or 65. A simple script works: "Do you offer a senior discount, and at what age?" Some stores only offer it on a set weekday. Some require a loyalty card. Membership groups such as AARP also negotiate discounts for members, so check before you book travel.

One caution. A discount is only a deal if you wanted the thing anyway. Be wary of anyone who calls you about a "senior discount" you never asked for. That is a common opening for a scam, and our scams guide explains why.

faq.q: Do I have to be a New Jersey resident for the State Park senior pass?
faq.a: Yes. The free Senior Citizen Pass is for New Jersey residents aged 62 or older. Bring ID showing your age and address to any state park office.

faq.q: Is the federal Senior Pass still $80?
faq.a: Yes. The lifetime Senior Pass is $80 and the annual Senior Pass is $20, for U.S. citizens or permanent residents aged 62 or older.

faq.q: Do I need a special card for NJ Transit senior fares?
faq.a: No. Any valid government, social service or transit ID with your date of birth works, including your Medicare card or driver's license. The reduced fare is half the regular one-way fare for riders 62 and older.

faq.q: Is college really free at 65?
faq.a: Tuition can be waived at New Jersey public colleges for residents 65 and older when seats are available, under N.J.S.A. 18A:62-3. You usually still pay fees, and you often may register only on or after the first day of classes. Ask the registrar how that school applies the waiver.

faq.q: Do seniors need a fishing license in New Jersey?
faq.a: New Jersey residents 70 and older do not need a freshwater fishing license or trout stamp. A driver's license or other proof of age serves as the license. Younger residents 16 and older need a license, and saltwater anglers 16 and older register with the state's saltwater registry.

faq.q: Which New Jersey museums are free to visit?
faq.a: The Princeton University Art Museum, the Zimmerli Art Museum at Rutgers and the New Jersey State Museum in Trenton all have free general admission. The State Museum charges for planetarium shows, with $1 off for seniors 65 and older.

title: 20 easy day trips in New Jersey, region by region
dek: Lighthouses, gardens, museums and wildlife drives, with honest notes on stairs, walking distances and the best season to go.
keyFacts: Cape May Lighthouse has 199 steps on its spiral staircase. The Oil House visitor center at its base is fully accessible.
Forsythe Refuge's 8-mile Wildlife Drive lets you birdwatch from your car for $4, and it honors the federal Senior Pass.
Duke Farms offers a free accessible shuttle to its Orchid Range by reservation.
East Point Lighthouse on the Delaware Bay reopens on a limited basis October 16, 2026.
NJ residents 62+ get free state park entrance with the Senior Citizen Pass.
body:
From almost any New Jersey town, a lighthouse, garden or good museum is an hour or two away. The trick is picking places that match your energy and your knees.

Each of these 20 trips works as an easy day. Where a site publishes step counts or accessibility services, we say so. Hours and fees change often, so check before you leave.

Before you go

Bring your free NJ State Park Senior Citizen Pass (residents 62+) and federal Senior Pass if you have one. See our guide to free and discounted things to do.

North Jersey

Thomas Edison National Historical Park, West Orange

Walk through Edison's real laboratory complex, including his library, chemistry lab and machine shop. A short drive away is Glenmont, his Victorian home in Llewellyn Park.

Getting around: An elevator serves the second and third floors of Building 5, the main lab. Free manual wheelchairs are available to borrow, first come, first served. Glenmont is not wheelchair accessible, and its tour has many steps, though you can view the house from accessible outdoor areas. Call the visitor desk at 973-736-0550 ext. 11.

Best time: Any time of year. Mostly indoors, so good on rainy days.

Paterson Great Falls National Historical Park, Paterson

See a 77-foot waterfall, 260 feet wide, in the heart of Paterson.

Getting around: Overlook Park, the main park address at 72 McBride Avenue Extension, has accessible parking. The Park Service says most areas are reachable on paved routes, and spots with outdoor stairs have a detour of about two minutes. Accessible restrooms are at the Paterson Museum, 2 Market Street. Walkways can close when they are icy or slippery.

Best time: After a few days of heavy rain, when the falls roar. In a deep freeze, the falls can partly ice over, which is a sight of its own.

New Jersey Botanical Garden at Skylands, Ringwood

Stroll formal gardens around Skylands Manor, a stone mansion in Ringwood State Park. The garden is on the State and National Registers of Historic Places, and volunteers lead periodic manor house tours.

Getting around: The garden opens at 8 a.m. and closes at 8 p.m. in daylight saving time and 6 p.m. the rest of the year. On summer weekends and holidays from Memorial Day weekend to Labor Day, there is a $5 state parking fee, cash only, for New Jersey vehicles. Terrain varies across the garden, so check the garden's parking and accessibility page for the easiest routes.

Best time: Late spring, when the gardens are at their fullest, and October for foliage.

Morristown National Historical Park and Frelinghuysen Arboretum, Morristown

Visit Washington's Headquarters Museum and tour the Ford Mansion, where George Washington spent the winter of 1779 to 1780. Finish at the nearby Frelinghuysen Arboretum.

Getting around: The museum and Jockey Hollow visitor center are open Thursday through Monday, 9:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Ford Mansion is by guided tour only, with free passes handed out at the museum desk, first come, first served. Ask about the tour route if stairs are a concern. The arboretum is open daily from 8 a.m. to sunset and has many paved trails.

Best time: Spring and fall. The arboretum's gardens are lovely from April through October.

Liberty State Park, Jersey City

Walk Liberty Walk, the waterfront promenade facing the Statue of Liberty and lower Manhattan. Visit Empty Sky, New Jersey's 9/11 memorial, and the restored Central Railroad of New Jersey Terminal, where ferries leave for Liberty and Ellis islands.

Getting around: The promenade is flat and paved. A free shuttle runs on weekends and holidays from April to November. Liberty Science Center, also in the park, is a good indoor backup.

Best time: A calm spring or fall day. Bring a layer for the wind.

Central Jersey

Grounds For Sculpture, Hamilton

Wander 42 acres of gardens filled with large outdoor sculpture, plus indoor galleries and places to eat.

Getting around: The main path is paver stone and accessible. Smaller paths are gravel or sand and can be uneven or steep. Wheelchairs rent for $15 a day and scooters for $29 for the first four hours, first come, first served, with ID. Access Mobile tours in ADA-rated vehicles cover the grounds in 45 minutes. Reserve at 609-586-0616. Check admission prices online before you go.

Best time: May and June for blooms, or a mild weekday in September or October.

Duke Farms, Hillsborough

Explore 2,700 acres on Doris Duke's former estate, with the glass Orchid Range as the highlight.

Getting around: Most of the trails are flat, paved and wide. A free Accessibility Transport service runs between the Farm Barn Orientation Center and the Orchid Range for people with limited mobility. Reservations are required. Saturday visits from April through October need a free parking pass, released Monday afternoons.

Best time: Spring for wildflowers and migrating birds. Weekdays avoid the Saturday parking pass entirely.

Princeton, Mercer County

Spend the morning at the free Princeton University Art Museum, then walk Nassau Street for lunch and bookshops.

Getting around: The museum is open daily, until 8 p.m. on Thursdays and Fridays. Its website lists accessibility and parking details.

Best time: Any season. A Thursday or Friday evening at the museum avoids weekend crowds.

New Jersey State Museum, Trenton

See natural history, art and state history, then catch a planetarium show.

Getting around: General admission is free. The museum is open Tuesday through Sunday, 9 a.m. to 4:45 p.m., at 205 West State Street. Planetarium tickets cost $10 for adults, with $1 off for seniors 65 and older.

Best time: Winter, or any rainy day.

Lambertville and the Delaware and Raritan Canal towpath, Hunterdon County

Browse antique shops in this river town, then walk the Delaware and Raritan Canal towpath. A bridge with a walkway crosses to New Hope, Pennsylvania.

Getting around: The towpath is level, which makes it one of the easiest long walks in the state. Walk out as far as you like and turn back.

Best time: October for river foliage, or a spring weekday.

Jersey Shore

Sandy Hook, Gateway National Recreation Area, Middletown

See the Sandy Hook Lighthouse, completed in 1764 and the oldest operating lighthouse in the nation. Walk the historic buildings of Fort Hancock and look across the bay to Manhattan.

Getting around: Lighthouse tours are seasonal and led by rangers. Sign up in person at the Sandy Hook Visitor Center on the day of your visit. The visitor center has been open Friday through Monday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The climb is 95 stairs and a 9-rung ladder, so many visitors happily stay on the ground. Call 732-872-5970 for tour times.

Best time: May, June, September and October, when beach traffic is light.

Twin Lights Historic Site, Highlands

This twin-towered lighthouse sits on a hill in Highlands with sweeping views over Sandy Hook Bay and the Atlantic. Look for the huge first-order Fresnel lens on display in the generator building.

Getting around: The views from the grounds are excellent without climbing anything. The north tower, the one open for climbing, has 64 steps with a landing about halfway up. From November 1 to Memorial Day the site is open Wednesday through Sunday, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Call 732-872-1814 before you go.

Best time: A clear fall day, when you can see the New York skyline.

Ocean Grove, Neptune Township

Walk the quiet boardwalk and Victorian streets of this camp meeting town. The centerpiece is the Great Auditorium, built in 1894. It seats about 7,000 and holds an organ with more than 11,000 pipes, one of the largest in the world.

Getting around: The boardwalk and town are flat. Many porches and inns have front steps, so plan your rest stops.

Best time: Summer for concerts and events in the Great Auditorium. September for warm, uncrowded beach walks.

Island Beach State Park, Berkeley Township

About 10 miles of undeveloped barrier island, with dunes, ocean beach and bay views. It is one of the last stretches of natural Jersey Shore.

Getting around: Beach wheelchairs, including ones fitted for surf fishing, are available at the two Bathing Beach Pavilions in summer and from the park office the rest of the year. Both pavilions have ramps. The Fisherman's Walkway at parking area A-7 is a wide boardwalk across the island. Call the park office at 732-793-0506.

Best time: September and early October, after summer fees and crowds fade.

Barnegat Lighthouse State Park, Barnegat Light, Long Beach Island

Visit "Old Barney," the red-and-white tower at the north tip of Long Beach Island, lit since 1859, and watch boats run Barnegat Inlet.

Getting around: The climb is 217 steps to the top. If that is too much, the grounds, the inlet views and the interpretive center are all at ground level.

Best time: Late spring or fall. Call ahead for climbing hours, which are seasonal.

South Jersey and the Delaware Bay

Cape May Lighthouse and Cape May Point State Park, Cape May Point

Climb or admire the 157-foot Cape May Lighthouse, then walk the park's nature trails and the beach. Add lunch in Victorian Cape May or the free Cape May County Park and Zoo.

Getting around: The climb is 199 steps on the original cast-iron spiral staircase. The Oil House at the base has a fully accessible orientation center and shop. Adult climbing tickets are $12. The zoo is open daily except Christmas, 10 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. in summer and to 3:30 p.m. in winter.

Best time: September and October, during fall bird migration, when Cape May is at its best and calmest.

Edwin B. Forsythe National Wildlife Refuge, Galloway

Drive the 8-mile Wildlife Drive through salt marsh, with the Atlantic City skyline across the water. The refuge sits on one of the busiest flight paths of the Atlantic Flyway.

Getting around: This is the best trip on the list for limited walking, because you can bird from your car. Entry is $4 per car, and the refuge honors America the Beautiful passes. Observation towers are at Gull Pond and Turtle Cove, and accessible restrooms are at headquarters. The drive is open sunrise to sunset.

Best time: Spring and fall migration. Bring binoculars.

Batsto Village, Wharton State Forest

Step into a restored 19th-century iron and glass village in the Pine Barrens, with a 36-room mansion, a general store, a sawmill and a nature center.

Getting around: The grounds are open dawn to dusk and the visitor center 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. Admission is free most days. Summer weekends carry a $5 fee for New Jersey residents. Call 609-561-0024 for mansion tour times and to ask about accessibility.

Best time: October, when the village hosts lantern tours, or December for holiday tours.

WheatonArts, Millville

Watch artists blow glass in the Glass Studio, then tour the Museum of American Glass and the artist studios.

Getting around: The campus opens April through December, Thursday through Sunday. WheatonArts asks guests who need accommodations to give two weeks' notice. Callers with hearing or speech disabilities can use NJ Relay at 711.

Best time: Spring and fall weekends, when demonstrations are in full swing.

East Point Lighthouse, Heislerville, Maurice River Township

This 1849 brick lighthouse on the Delaware Bay reopens to the public on a limited basis on October 16, 2026, after being closed since 2024. Admission is free for now. County officials expect to expand hours once a fuller plan for programs is in place early next year.

Getting around: Hours are limited at first, so check with Cumberland County tourism before you drive down.

Best time: Late fall now, then May and June, when shorebirds and horseshoe crabs gather on the Delaware Bay beaches.

How do I plan an easy day?

  1. Call ahead. Ask three questions: Where is the closest accessible parking? Are there wheelchairs or shuttles? Where are the restrooms?
  2. Pick one main stop. One destination and a sit-down lunch beats three rushed stops.
  3. Go midweek. Parking is easier, lines are shorter and staff have more time to help.
  4. Pack for the weather. Shore sites are windier and cooler than inland towns. Bring water, a hat and a light jacket.

Prefer a group? Many senior centers run bus trips. See our guide to staying connected.

faq.q: Which of these trips involves the least walking?
faq.a: The Forsythe Refuge Wildlife Drive, which you see from your car. Duke Farms and Grounds For Sculpture also offer accessible transport or tours by reservation.

faq.q: How many steps is the Cape May Lighthouse?
faq.a: 199 steps on the original cast-iron spiral staircase. The Oil House at the base has a fully accessible orientation center if you would rather stay on the ground.

faq.q: Is the East Point Lighthouse open?
faq.a: It reopens on a limited basis on October 16, 2026, with free admission for now. Hours are expected to grow in early 2027, so check before you go.

faq.q: Do my senior passes work at these places?
faq.a: The New Jersey State Park Senior Citizen Pass gives residents 62+ free entrance to state parks. The federal Senior Pass covers entrance at federal sites that charge fees, such as the Forsythe Refuge.

faq.q: Which New Jersey lighthouses can I enjoy without climbing?
faq.a: All of them. Cape May, Barnegat, Sandy Hook and Twin Lights have grounds, views and exhibits at ground level. Twin Lights in Highlands is the easiest climb if you do want to go up, at 64 steps.

title: Learn something new after 60: classes and lessons across New Jersey
dek: From Osher courses at Rutgers to piano lessons in your own living room, here is where older New Jerseyans can keep learning, and why stretching your brain is worth it.
keyFacts: OLLI at Rutgers offers noncredit courses for adults 50+ with no tests or grades.
Bergen Community College's Institute for Learning in Retirement is open to adults 55+ for $150 a semester.
NJ public colleges can waive tuition for residents 65+ when seats are open (N.J.S.A. 18A:62-3).
In the Synapse Project, older adults who learned demanding new skills showed memory gains that a social-only group did not.
Senior Planet's free tech hotline: 888-713-3495.
body:
Plenty of people stop learning on purpose after they leave school or work. Then one day they pick up a guitar, sign up for a history course or start Italian before a trip, and remember how good it feels.

New Jersey makes this easy. There are university programs built for older learners, community college courses, library classes and teachers who will come to your home. This guide walks through each option, what it costs and how to start.

Does learning something hard really help the brain?

One of the best-known studies on this question came out of the University of Texas at Dallas. It is called the Synapse Project, led by psychologist Denise Park and published in the journal Psychological Science in 2014.

Researchers assigned 221 adults aged 60 to 90 to spend about 15 hours a week, for three months, on different activities. Some learned digital photography. Some learned quilting on computerized sewing machines. Some did both. Other groups met for social activities like games and outings, or did easy tasks at home, such as listening to music and doing simple word puzzles.

The people who learned demanding new skills, particularly digital photography, showed significant improvements in memory. The social group and the easy-tasks group did not. Park's takeaway was simple. Activities need to be new and mentally challenging to have this effect. Being busy or social is good for you in other ways, but it is a different thing.

Comfortable hobbies are lovely. Hard new skills are where the brain gets a workout.

Why would photography beat a social club? Learning a camera means juggling new vocabulary, menus and techniques, and holding them in memory while you practice. That kind of sustained effort is what the researchers believed made the difference.

Keep this in perspective. It was one study with a few hundred people, and it does not prove that piano lessons prevent dementia. It does suggest a useful rule: choose something that makes you a little uncomfortable, and stick with it for months.

Where can I take college-style courses with no exams?

Osher Lifelong Learning Institute at Rutgers (OLLI-RU)

Osher Lifelong Learning Institutes are member-driven programs at universities around the country, funded in part by the Bernard Osher Foundation. New Jersey's is at Rutgers. OLLI-RU serves adults 50 and older with noncredit courses. There are no tests and no grades. The atmosphere is friendly and informal.

In-person classes in New Brunswick meet on the first floor of the Rutgers Lifelong Learning Center at 3 Rutgers Plaza, which the program describes as completely accessible. Registered students park free in the university lot with an electronic permit, sent by email about a week before classes start. OLLI-RU publishes seasonal catalogs for fall, winter, spring and summer. Membership is optional. It costs $50 a year and gets you member course rates and longer refund windows. Call 848-932-6554 or visit olliru.rutgers.edu.

Institute for Learning in Retirement, Bergen Community College

Bergen's ILR is open to anyone 55 or older. You do not need a degree, and you do not need to be retired. Membership is $150 per semester and lets you take up to four multi-week courses plus three shorter bonus sessions. Classes meet at the Paramus campus or online, with no tests or grades. Register at 201-447-7156.

Evergreen Forum in Princeton

The Center for Modern Aging Princeton runs the Evergreen Forum, peer-led courses in literature, art, politics, history and science. Courses run three to eight weeks, in person or online. Current fees are $95 for a three- or four-week course and $125 for a five- to eight-week course. The center has offered senior scholarships for people who find the fee a hardship, so ask. Registration is first come, first served and fills quickly, so get on the mailing list.

Adult schools

Many towns run adult schools through the local school district. The Princeton Adult School, for example, offered more than 300 in-person and virtual classes in spring 2025. Check your town or the next town over. Classes are usually short, cheap and close to home.

Can I sit in on regular college classes?

Yes. New Jersey law, N.J.S.A. 18A:62-3, lets public colleges and universities waive tuition for residents 65 and older. Seats must be available, and fees usually still apply. Many schools only let seniors register on or after the first day of classes. Each campus sets its own rules, so call the registrar first.

Community colleges are the friendliest place to start. They are close to home, parking is easy and classes run from accounting to watercolor. Most also run noncredit continuing education with personal-interest courses in cooking, photography, languages and fitness. Our guide to free and discounted things to do explains the tuition waiver in more detail.

What does each option cost?

Prices change each term, so treat these as a starting point and confirm before you register.

OptionWho can joinCost
OLLI at RutgersAdults 50+Optional $50 yearly membership, plus course fees
Bergen ILRAdults 55+$150 per semester for up to four courses and three bonus sessions
Evergreen Forum, PrincetonOlder adults$95 or $125 per course, depending on length
Public college coursesNJ residents 65+Tuition may be waived when seats are open. Fees still apply.
Senior Planet from AARPAnyoneFree classes and tech hotline
Public library programsCardholdersUsually free

A worked example helps. Say you are 67 and live in Paramus. One semester at the Bergen ILR costs $150 and can cover four courses. A single Evergreen Forum course runs $95 to $125 for several weeks of classes in Princeton or online. Auditing a Spanish class at your county college under the senior waiver could cost only the fees. Mix a free option with one paid one, and see which you still look forward to by November.

What do libraries offer?

Your public library is a free classroom. Most New Jersey libraries offer some mix of book clubs, author talks, art workshops, local history lectures, knitting circles and technology help. Many also give cardholders free access to online learning services, including language courses and video classes. Ask a librarian what your card includes. You may be surprised.

For technology, Senior Planet from AARP is excellent. It offers free online classes on everything from smartphones to video calls, and a free tech hotline at 888-713-3495, open Monday through Saturday in English, Spanish and Mandarin. Callers who need more help can book a free one-on-one video session with a volunteer.

How do I pick music, art or a language?

Think about what you will still want to do in month three, when the novelty wears off. A few questions help:

  • Do you want company? Choirs, community bands, drawing groups and conversation tables give you friends along with skills.
  • Do you want a goal? Learning a language for a trip, or a song for a grandchild's birthday, keeps you practicing.
  • What does your body allow? Arthritis in the hands may point toward voice, drawing with thicker tools or a keyboard with lighter keys. Ask a teacher to adapt.
  • How much can you practice? Twenty minutes most days beats two hours once a week.

Some New Jersey options to look for: community bands and choruses that welcome adult beginners, county arts councils that list classes, art centers with weekday studio courses, and library conversation groups for English and other languages. A college course in Spanish or Italian, taken under the senior tuition waiver, is another affordable path.

Beginners are welcome almost everywhere. The hardest part is usually walking in the door for the first lesson. Tell the teacher you are starting from zero, and let them set the pace.

Common mistakes

Signing up for too much at once and burning out. Picking only what you already know. Quitting after a hard week. Paying for a long package before trying one class. Start small, choose something new and give it a full season.

What if I can't get to a class?

Driving at night, mobility problems or caring for a spouse can make classes hard to reach. The answer may be bringing the teacher to you. Private lessons at home let you learn at your own pace, in a familiar room, with no stairs to climb or parking to find.

In Essex County, Home Happenings sends local teachers to people's homes for lessons in piano, guitar, painting, yoga and more. It is one example of a growing kind of service built for people who want to keep learning while aging in place. Elsewhere, ask at your library, a local music store or your senior center for teachers who travel.

Hiring a teacher for home lessons

Ask for references and how long they have taught adults. Ask whether they are insured and background-checked. Agree on the price, length and cancellation rules in writing. Start with one trial lesson before buying a package.

  1. Pick one thing. Choose a skill that is new and a bit hard.
  2. Find the format. Class, club, online or at home.
  3. Commit to a season. Sign up for a full term or eight to twelve lessons.
  4. Bring a friend. A partner makes you more likely to keep showing up.
  5. Check in at three months. Notice what you can do now that you could not do before.

Whatever you choose, tell people about it. Saying "I'm learning the guitar" out loud tends to keep you practicing, and it gives friends and grandchildren something new to ask you about.

Learning is also one of the easiest ways to meet people. For more on that, read our guide to staying connected in New Jersey, and for brain and body health more broadly, see healthy aging in New Jersey.

faq.q: Who can join OLLI at Rutgers?
faq.a: OLLI-RU serves adults 50 and older. Courses are noncredit with no tests or grades. Call 848-932-6554 or visit olliru.rutgers.edu for the current catalog and fees.

faq.q: Can I take college classes for free at 65 in New Jersey?
faq.a: Public colleges may waive tuition for residents 65 and older when space is available, under N.J.S.A. 18A:62-3. You usually still pay fees, and registration is often limited to the first day of classes or later.

faq.q: What did the Synapse Project find?
faq.a: In a 2014 study in Psychological Science, adults 60 to 90 who spent about 15 hours a week for three months learning demanding new skills, particularly digital photography, showed memory improvements. Groups doing social or easy activities did not.

faq.q: Where can I get free help learning my phone or computer?
faq.a: Try your public library, or call the Senior Planet from AARP tech hotline at 888-713-3495, Monday through Saturday.

faq.q: How much does the Bergen Community College Institute for Learning in Retirement cost?
faq.a: Membership is $150 per semester and is not refundable. It covers up to four primary courses and three bonus courses, and members must be 55 or older.

faq.q: Do I need a degree or need to be retired to join a lifelong learning program?
faq.a: No. Programs such as OLLI at Rutgers and the Bergen ILR have no degree requirement, no tests and no grades. At Bergen you must be 55 or older, but you do not need to be retired.

title: Staying connected: how to beat loneliness in New Jersey
dek: Loneliness is a health risk, and the U.S. Surgeon General has said so plainly. Here are the senior centers, volunteer roles, phone and visitor programs, and tech help that can bring more people into your week.
keyFacts: The Surgeon General's 2023 advisory says lacking social connection can raise the risk of early death as much as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.
Chronic loneliness and isolation can raise dementia risk by about 50% in older adults, the advisory says.
Find your senior center through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 or by dialing 2-1-1.
NJ SHIP trains volunteers to counsel people on Medicare: 1-800-792-8820.
Senior Planet's free tech hotline: 888-713-3495.
body:
Loneliness tends to arrive quietly. A spouse dies. Friends move to Florida or to their children's towns. You stop driving at night, and then the Tuesday card game fades away. None of it is anyone's fault, and all of it adds up.

The good news is that New Jersey is full of ways back in. This guide covers the research on why connection matters, then the practical places to find it, from your senior center to a daily phone call from a volunteer.

What did the Surgeon General say about loneliness?

In May 2023, U.S. Surgeon General Vivek Murthy issued an advisory called Our Epidemic of Loneliness and Isolation. Advisories are reserved for urgent public health issues. A few of its findings stand out for older adults:

  • In recent years, about one in two adults in America reported experiencing loneliness.
  • Lacking social connection can increase the risk of premature death as much as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day.
  • Poor social relationships were linked to a 29% higher risk of heart disease and a 32% higher risk of stroke.
  • Chronic loneliness and social isolation can increase the risk of developing dementia by about 50% in older adults.
  • The highest rates of social isolation are found among older adults.

Two words in that report are worth separating. Isolation is how many contacts you have. Loneliness is how you feel about them. You can live alone and feel fine, or sit at a crowded family dinner and feel alone. Both matter, and both can change.

Loneliness is a health risk. Treat a lonely stretch the way you would treat high blood pressure: notice it, and do something about it.

Where do I start?

Start with your local senior center. Most New Jersey towns or counties run one, and they are far livelier than their reputation. Expect exercise classes, lunch programs, cards and mah-jongg, lectures, crafts, day trips and health screenings. Many are free or nearly free for residents.

To find yours, call the statewide Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737. It routes you to your county office on aging, which knows every center, club and program nearby. You can also dial 2-1-1 or 1-800-510-3102 for NJ 211.

  1. Get the calendar. Ask the center to mail or email the monthly schedule.
  2. Choose one activity. Something with a set time each week works best, such as a class or a lunch.
  3. Go three times. The first visit is awkward for everyone. By the third, people know your name.
  4. Ask about rides. Many counties offer senior transportation to centers and programs.

How can volunteering help?

Volunteering gives you a reason to leave the house, a team to belong to and the feeling of being needed. These programs in New Jersey welcome older volunteers.

AARP Foundation Tax-Aide

Tax-Aide volunteers prepare free tax returns at libraries, senior centers and town halls. You do not need a tax or financial background. Volunteers serve as tax preparers or as client facilitators who greet and organize, and they get training on federal and New Jersey tax law. Bilingual volunteers are especially needed. Recruiting happens in late summer for the next tax season, so apply early through AARP's Tax-Aide page. In Somerset County, for example, volunteers for the coming tax season were asked to apply by September 1, 2026, so they could finish a background check before training.

SHIP Medicare counselors

New Jersey's State Health Insurance Assistance Program (SHIP) gives free, unbiased Medicare counseling, and it relies on trained volunteers. If you understand Medicare, or want to, this is meaningful work. Call 1-800-792-8820 to ask about volunteering. Counselors do not sell or endorse any insurance product.

AmeriCorps Seniors RSVP

RSVP matches volunteers aged 55 and older with local nonprofits. In Gloucester County, the RSVP program based in West Deptford places volunteers about three to four hours a week and runs its own programs, including SHIP counseling and a Friendly Caller/Visitor service for homebound seniors. Call 856-468-1742. In Morris County, Norwescap's RSVP program in Morristown has recruited volunteers 55 and older to make scheduled telephone reassurance calls. Call 973-784-4900. Federal funding for AmeriCorps programs has shifted in recent years, so ask your county office on aging which RSVP programs are active near you.

Food banks and pantries

New Jersey's regional food banks, including the Community FoodBank of New Jersey, Fulfill in Monmouth and Ocean counties, Mercer Street Friends and the Food Bank of South Jersey, all rely on volunteers to sort, pack and distribute food. Many offer weekday shifts that suit retirees. Local pantries at churches and synagogues need help too.

What if I can't get out much?

If health, weather or caregiving keeps you home, connection can come to you. Two kinds of programs exist for exactly this.

Telephone reassurance means a trained volunteer calls you at a set time, often daily, to check in and chat. If you do not answer, the program follows emergency steps. In Union County, Catholic Charities of the Archdiocese of Newark runs a free telephone reassurance program for older adults who live alone. Call 908-709-9580, weekdays 8:30 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.

Friendly visitors are volunteers who come to your home for conversation, cards or a walk. Programs exist through Meals on Wheels in Greater New Brunswick, Jewish Family Service of Somerset, Hunterdon and Warren Counties, and the Gloucester County RSVP program, among others. Visitors in these programs are usually screened and trained.

Every county has something similar. Call your county office on aging through the ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 and ask, "Do you have a friendly visitor or telephone reassurance program?"

For adult children

Watch for signs of isolation: fewer mentions of friends, skipped activities, unopened mail, changes in eating. Set up a weekly video call at a fixed time. Help a parent get to one activity in person, and go with them the first time. Our guide to the first conversation about care can help you raise it gently.

Can technology help?

Video calls, family group texts and online classes can fill the gaps between visits. The barrier is often just setup. Senior Planet from AARP offers free online classes and a free tech hotline at 888-713-3495, Monday through Saturday, in English, Spanish and Mandarin. Callers who need more help can book a free one-on-one video session with a volunteer. Senior Planet also hosts online exercise, crafting hangouts and discussion groups.

Your public library is the other great tech resource. Many offer one-on-one help with phones and tablets, and some lend devices or hotspots. Ask what your library offers.

A word of caution: online is also where scammers look for lonely people. If a new online friend asks for money, stop. Read our guide to scams before you join dating sites or new social apps.

What about clubs, faith communities and pets?

Clubs. Garden clubs, book groups, walking groups, model railroaders, bird clubs, community choirs and veterans' posts all meet regularly and welcome new members. Classes count too. Our guide to learning something new lists programs like OLLI at Rutgers that double as social clubs.

Younger people. Friendships across generations count. Tutoring at a school, reading programs at the library and mentoring through local nonprofits put you in regular contact with kids and young adults, which many older volunteers find energizing.

Faith communities. Churches, synagogues, mosques and temples often run senior groups, meal programs and visiting ministries for members who are homebound. If you have drifted away from a congregation, a call to the office is often welcomed.

Pets. A dog gets you outside and talking to neighbors. A cat gives a quiet house some company. Before adopting, think honestly about cost, mobility and who would care for the animal if you were hospitalized. Many shelters have older, calmer animals that suit older owners, and some let you foster before you commit. If you cannot keep a pet, shelters need volunteers to walk dogs and socialize cats.

What does a one-month plan look like?

Big resolutions fade. Small, scheduled habits stick. Here is a simple four-week plan you can adapt.

  1. Week one: make two calls. Call your county office on aging through the ADRC and ask for the senior center calendar. Then call one old friend you have not spoken to in a while.
  2. Week two: show up once. Go to one class, lunch or club meeting. Sit near the front, and ask one person how long they have been coming.
  3. Week three: add a weekly anchor. Pick something with a fixed day and time, such as a Tuesday exercise class or a Thursday book group, and put it on your calendar.
  4. Week four: give something. Ask about one volunteer role, even a few hours a month. Being needed is one of the strongest cures for feeling alone.

If getting out is not realistic, swap in a telephone reassurance program, a weekly video call with family and an online Senior Planet class. The point is a regular rhythm of contact, wherever it happens.

When loneliness feels heavier

Sometimes loneliness slides into depression. Signs include losing interest in things you used to enjoy, sleeping much more or less, and feeling hopeless for weeks. Tell your doctor, who can screen for depression and refer you to counseling. Medicare covers a yearly depression screening and mental health visits. If you or someone you love is in crisis, call or text 988 for the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, any time.

Pick one idea from this page and try it this week. Connection is built one small, repeated habit at a time.

faq.q: What did the Surgeon General's 2023 advisory say?
faq.a: It said about one in two U.S. adults reported loneliness in recent years, and that lacking social connection can raise the risk of premature death as much as smoking up to 15 cigarettes a day. It also linked chronic loneliness and isolation to about a 50% higher risk of dementia in older adults.

faq.q: How do I find a senior center near me in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the Aging and Disability Resource Connection at 1-877-222-3737 to reach your county office on aging, or dial 2-1-1.

faq.q: Is there a program that will call me every day?
faq.a: Yes. Many counties have telephone reassurance programs. In Union County, Catholic Charities of the Archdiocese of Newark offers free daily calls to older adults who live alone (908-709-9580). Ask your county office on aging about others.

faq.q: Can I volunteer if I have no special skills?
faq.a: Yes. AARP Tax-Aide needs greeters as well as preparers, food banks need packers, and telephone reassurance programs train callers. RSVP programs match adults 55 and older with local roles.

faq.q: What is a telephone reassurance program?
faq.a: A trained volunteer calls an older adult at a set time, often daily, to check in and chat. If no one answers, the program follows emergency steps. Ask your county office on aging through 1-877-222-3737 whether one serves your town.

faq.q: Does Medicare cover help for depression?
faq.a: Yes. Medicare covers a yearly depression screening in a primary care setting and outpatient mental health visits. Tell your doctor if loneliness has turned into weeks of low mood or lost interest.

title: Scams targeting New Jersey seniors now, and how to shut them down
dek: Fake grandkids, fake toll bills, fake PSE&G shutoffs. Learn the scripts scammers use, the red flags that give them away, and exactly who to call in New Jersey if money is already gone.
keyFacts: People 60+ reported $7.7 billion in losses to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center in 2025.
NJ Division of Consumer Affairs complaints: 1-800-242-5846.
New Jersey E-ZPass does not send unsolicited texts asking you to pay tolls.
PSE&G will never ask for payment in gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency, or demand payment on the spot.
Credit freezes are free at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion.
body:
Scammers love older adults for one reason. That is where the savings are. They are organized, patient and very good at sounding official. Smart, careful people fall for them every day.

The numbers keep climbing. People aged 60 and older reported $7.7 billion in losses to the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) in 2025, about 60% more than in 2024. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) counted $4.3 billion in reported losses for people 50 and older in 2025. Most fraud is never reported, so the real totals are higher.

This guide covers the scams hitting New Jersey right now, the words they use and what to do the moment something feels wrong.

What are the most common scams right now?

The grandparent or family emergency scam

The script: "Grandma, it's me. I was in an accident and I'm in jail. Please don't tell Mom." A second voice then plays a lawyer or police officer and asks for bail money. Some scammers now send a courier or rideshare driver to your door to pick up cash. Others ask you to mail cash hidden in a package.

The tell: secrecy and speed. Hang up and call your grandchild or their parent at a number you already know. Families can agree on a code word that only real relatives would know.

Medicare scams

The script: "This is Medicare. You are due a new card," or "You qualify for a free back brace, genetic test or glucose monitor. I just need your Medicare number." These spike during open enrollment, which runs October 15 to December 7.

The tell: Medicare does not call to sell you anything or visit your home. Only give your Medicare number to your doctors, insurers acting for you or your SHIP counselor. Read every Medicare Summary Notice and look for services you never got.

Tech support scams

The script: A pop-up freezes your screen with a loud alarm and a number to call "Microsoft" or "Apple." Or a caller says your computer is infected. They ask to take remote control, then "find" problems, or say your bank account is hacked and you must move money to a "safe" account.

The tell: Real tech companies do not cold call you or put phone numbers in pop-up warnings. Never let a stranger take control of your computer. Shut it down and restart.

Toll and E-ZPass text scams

The script: "NJ E-ZPass: You have an unpaid toll balance of $6.99. Pay now to avoid a late fee" with a link.

The tell: New Jersey officials say NJ E-ZPass does not send unsolicited texts asking for toll payments. The one exception is an account already in collections, where Credit Collection Services may text a phone number, the site ccspayment.com and a file number. Do not click. Log in to your E-ZPass account directly to check.

Utility shutoff scams

The script: "This is PSE&G. Your power will be shut off within the hour unless you pay now." The caller ID may even show PSE&G.

The tell: PSE&G says a real representative will identify themselves, reference your account details and never ask for payment on the spot. It will never ask for payment in gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency, and it will never pressure you to pay within the hour. Anyone demanding a prepaid debit card, gift card or crypto is a scammer. Hang up and call PSE&G at 1-800-436-7734. If you truly are behind, ask about assistance programs, and see our guide to food and utility help.

Romance scams

The script: A warm, attentive new friend online, often a widower, soldier overseas, oil rig worker or doctor abroad. Weeks of daily messages. Then a crisis: customs fees, a medical bill, a frozen account.

The tell: They always have a reason they cannot video chat or meet. Anyone you have never met in person who asks for money is a scammer. IC3 recorded $929 million in romance scam losses across all ages in 2025.

Investment and crypto scams

The script: A friendly stranger, sometimes from a "wrong number" text, introduces you to a trading app with amazing returns. You see your balance grow, but you can never withdraw.

The tell: Guaranteed high returns, pressure to buy cryptocurrency and a platform you cannot find independently. Cryptocurrency-related fraud led all categories in IC3 losses in 2025, at $11.3 billion across all ages.

Gift card scams

Gift cards show up in nearly every scam above. No real government agency, utility, police department or company will ever ask you to pay with a gift card. If someone tells you to buy gift cards and read them the numbers, it is a scam, every time.

What should I say when a scammer calls?

Most people freeze because they do not want to be rude. You do not owe a stranger politeness. It helps to have a few lines ready, the way you would rehearse a fire drill.

Lines that end the call

"I don't handle that by phone. I'll call the number on my statement." "I never confirm personal information on a call I didn't make." "I'm going to hang up and call my grandson myself." Then hang up. You do not need to explain or argue.

Here is how it plays out. Say a caller tells you your Medicare card is expiring and asks you to read your number to "keep coverage active." You say your line about calling the number yourself, hang up and dial 1-800-MEDICARE from the back of your card. Medicare does not call to sell you anything or visit your home, so you will learn in two minutes that nothing is wrong.

Write your lines on an index card and keep it by the phone. Put your bank's fraud number, your children's numbers and the Elder Fraud Hotline on the same card.

What are the red flags?

  • Urgency. "Right now," "within the hour," "before the bank closes."
  • Secrecy. "Don't tell anyone," "don't tell the bank teller why."
  • Odd payment. Gift cards, wire transfers, crypto, a Bitcoin ATM, payment apps or cash handed to a courier.
  • Fear or excitement. Arrest, shutoff, a hacked account, a prize, a big return.
  • They contacted you. Unexpected calls, texts, emails and pop-ups.
Hang up, slow down and call someone you trust. A real emergency will still be real in ten minutes.

I already paid. What do I do now?

Act fast and do not let embarrassment slow you down. Speed is what gets money back.

  1. Call the company you paid through. Your bank or credit card company for a card, transfer or Zelle payment. The gift card company, using the number on the back of the card, for gift cards. Ask them to stop or reverse the payment.
  2. Change passwords. If you gave remote access to a computer, have it checked and change passwords from a different device.
  3. Report it. File with the agencies in the next section. Reports help investigators trace money and warn others.
  4. Watch for recovery scams. Scammers often call victims back pretending to be lawyers or agents who can recover your money for a fee. That is a second scam.
  5. Get help. The U.S. Department of Justice's National Elder Fraud Hotline, 1-833-372-8311 (1-833-FRAUD-11), helps people 60 and older report fraud and find next steps, weekdays 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern.

If your Social Security number or Medicare number was stolen, go to IdentityTheft.gov for a recovery plan.

Where do I report a scam in New Jersey?

WhereWhat forHow
NJ Division of Consumer AffairsScams and consumer fraud in New Jersey1-800-242-5846 (in NJ) or 973-504-6200, or online
Federal Trade CommissionAny scam or fraudreportfraud.ftc.gov
FBI Internet Crime Complaint CenterOnline, text, crypto and investment fraudic3.gov
Local policeAny loss, and required by some banksNon-emergency number, or 911 if a courier is coming
NJ Senior Medicare PatrolMedicare and Medicaid fraud1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117
MedicareSuspicious charges or calls1-800-633-4227 (1-800-MEDICARE)

Call 1-800-242-5846 for the Division of Consumer Affairs and 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117 for Senior Medicare Patrol. If an older person is being exploited by someone they know, such as a relative, caregiver or new "friend," contact your county's Adult Protective Services. The ADRC at 1-877-222-3737 can connect you.

How do I protect my accounts?

Freeze your credit. A credit freeze stops anyone from opening new credit in your name. It is free at all three bureaus: Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It does not affect your credit score or your existing cards. You can lift it when you need to apply for credit.

Name a trusted contact. Brokerage firms must make reasonable efforts to collect the name of a trusted contact person under FINRA Rule 4512. That person cannot trade or move money. The firm can call them if it cannot reach you or suspects exploitation. Under FINRA Rule 2165, a firm that suspects exploitation can place a temporary hold on a disbursement. After a recent amendment, the hold can last up to 55 business days in total when the firm has reported the matter to Adult Protective Services, law enforcement or a court. Ask your bank whether it offers something similar.

Set up account alerts. Turn on text or email alerts for withdrawals, large purchases and password changes.

Check Medicare claims. Create a secure account at Medicare.gov to see Original Medicare claims as soon as they are processed.

Screen your calls. Let unknown numbers go to voicemail. Real callers leave messages.

For adult children

Talk about scams before one happens, the way you would talk about a fire plan. Agree on a family code word. Offer to be the person your parent calls before sending money to anyone. Read our guide to estate planning in New Jersey for powers of attorney that protect a parent later on.

Being targeted is not a sign of weakness. It is a sign that criminals are working hard. The best defense is a habit: pause, hang up and check with someone you trust.

faq.q: What number do I call to report a scam in New Jersey?
faq.a: Call the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs at 1-800-242-5846 (in New Jersey) or 973-504-6200, or file online. Also report to the FTC at reportfraud.ftc.gov and, for online or crypto fraud, to the FBI at ic3.gov.

faq.q: Does NJ E-ZPass text me about unpaid tolls?
faq.a: New Jersey officials say NJ E-ZPass does not send unsolicited texts asking for toll payment. The exception is accounts in collections, where Credit Collection Services may text. Check your account directly instead of clicking any link.

faq.q: Will PSE&G call and threaten to shut off my power today?
faq.a: PSE&G says real representatives identify themselves, reference your account details and never ask for payment on the spot. It never asks for gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency. Hang up and call PSE&G at 1-800-436-7734.

faq.q: Is a credit freeze free?
faq.a: Yes. Freezing and lifting your credit is free at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. You need to place a freeze with each bureau.

faq.q: Who handles Medicare fraud in New Jersey?
faq.a: The NJ Senior Medicare Patrol at 1-732-777-1940 ext. 1117. You can also call 1-800-MEDICARE (1-800-633-4227).

faq.q: What is the National Elder Fraud Hotline?
faq.a: It is a free U.S. Department of Justice hotline for people 60 and older and their families. Call 1-833-372-8311 (1-833-FRAUD-11), Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. Eastern, for help reporting fraud and finding next steps.
